claim: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Purkinje cells (PC), the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, encode sensorimotor information, but how they do it remains a matter of debate.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Purkinje cells encode sensorimotor information.
source: Purkinje cells (PC), the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, encode sensorimotor information, but how they do it remains a matter of debate.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, though the mechanism is debated.

claim: Purkinje cells use a multiplexed spike code.
source: Here we show that PCs use a multiplexed spike code.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Synchrony/spike time and firing rate encode different information in Purkinje cells during saccadic eye motion tasks.
source: Synchrony/spike time and firing rate encode different information in behaving monkeys during saccadic eye motion tasks.
evidence: This is a main finding supported by experimental data from monkey recordings.

claim: Pause spikes provide a temporally reliable signal for eye motion onset.
source: we found that infrequent pause spikes, which initiated or terminated intermittent pauses in simple spike trains, provide a temporally reliable signal for eye motion onset, with strong phase-coupling to the β/γ band LFP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing spike reliability and phase-coupling measurements.

claim: Pause spikes have strong phase-coupling to the β/γ band LFP.
source: we found that infrequent pause spikes, which initiated or terminated intermittent pauses in simple spike trains, provide a temporally reliable signal for eye motion onset, with strong phase-coupling to the β/γ band LFP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PPC measurements and phase distribution analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Non-pause spikes are weakly correlated with the LFP.
source: Concurrently, regularly firing, non-pause spikes were weakly correlated with the LFP, but were crucial to linear encoding of eye movement kinematics by firing rate.
evidence: This is shown by STALFP analysis in Figure 3A showing weak modulation for regular spikes.

claim: Regular spikes are crucial to linear encoding of eye movement kinematics by firing rate.
source: Concurrently, regularly firing, non-pause spikes were weakly correlated with the LFP, but were crucial to linear encoding of eye movement kinematics by firing rate.
evidence: This is supported by the linear-nonlinear model analysis in Figure 5 showing high R² values for regular spikes.

claim: PC spike trains can simultaneously convey information necessary to achieve precision in both timing and continuous control of motion.
source: Therefore, PC spike trains can simultaneously convey information necessary to achieve precision in both timing and continuous control of motion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the multiplexed coding findings.

claim: The cerebellum is heavily involved in online motor control.
source: The cerebellum is heavily involved in online motor control and should process sensorimotor information with great accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Precisely timed PC spikes and their synchronized firing can transmit timing-sensitive information.
source: In one view, transmission of timing-sensitive information is performed by precisely timed PC spikes and their synchronized firing (Ebner and Bloedel, 1981; Gauck and Jaeger, 2000; Shin and De Schutter, 2006; de Solages et al., 2008; De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Person and Raman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PCs use linear firing-rate coding with weak PC-to-PC correlations to robustly control continuous movement kinematics.
source: In the other, PCs use linear firing-rate coding with weak PC-to-PC correlations to robustly control continuous movement kinematics, where high signal-to-noise ratio is achieved by averaging the rates of many PCs (Shidara et al., 1993; Thier et al., 2000; Roitman et al., 2005; Medina and Lisberger, 2007; Catz et al., 2008; Herzfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an alternative view supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pauses in the PC spike train abruptly interrupt the rapid and very regular firing of PCs.
source: In particular, we focused on the role of long, infrequent interspike intervals (ISI), called pauses, which abruptly interrupt the rapid and very regular firing of PCs (Schonewille et al., 2006; Shin and De Schutter, 2006; Shin et al., 2007; Yartsev et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spikes that initiate and terminate pauses often synchronize sharply across nearby PCs.
source: Spikes that initiate and terminate pauses often synchronize sharply across nearby PCs (Shin and De Schutter, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recordings were obtained from three rhesus (Macaca mulatta) monkeys.
source: From three rhesus (Macaca mulatta) monkeys (E, H, and N), we simultaneously recorded spikes of single PCs, the slow component of the LFP below low-γ frequency (42 Hz), and eye positions during spontaneous and visually guided saccades (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Only recordings where both simple and complex spikes could be isolated were used.
source: Only recordings where both simple and complex spikes could be isolated were used.
evidence: This describes a selection criterion for the data analysis.

claim: Complex spikes comprised 1.71 ± 0.13% of total spikes with a rate of 0.81 ± 0.07 Hz.
source: In this study, we focused exclusively on simple spikes, since complex spikes comprised a very small percentage of total spikes (1.71 ± 0.13% with a rate of 0.81 ± 0.07 Hz, mean ± SEM) and their overall effect on firing statistics was not significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, see also below).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: CCFLFP-EV was significant in recordings from 49 cells.
source: First, CCFLFP-EV was significant in recordings from 49 cells (p<0.01, t-test, n = 33, 15, 1 from E, H, and N, respectively), but significant CCFSpike-EV was found only in a subset of 34 cells (p<0.01, t-test, n = 21, 12, 1 from E, H, and N, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Significant CCFSpike-EV was found only in a subset of 34 cells.
source: First, CCFLFP-EV was significant in recordings from 49 cells (p<0.01, t-test, n = 33, 15, 1 from E, H, and N, respectively), but significant CCFSpike-EV was found only in a subset of 34 cells (p<0.01, t-test, n = 21, 12, 1 from E, H, and N, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The CCF varied less significantly with the angles of eye movements for the LFP than for spikes in most cases.
source: Second, when computed to account for the eye speed component for specific directions, the CCF varied less significantly with the angles of eye movements for the LFP than for spikes, in most cases (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C where 74% of recordings showed this pattern.

claim: The LFP represents the average activity of many neurons with diverse angle-dependencies in the local network.
source: This supports the view that the LFP represents the average activity of many neurons with diverse angle-dependencies in the local network (Buzsáki et al., 2012) rather than reflecting the activity of a single PC or a cluster of PCs with similar directional tuning.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by a citation and by the observed differences in directional tuning.

claim: All recorded PCs fired rapidly at 55 ± 18 Hz with high regularity.
source: All recorded PCs fired rapidly (55 ± 18 Hz, mean ± SD) with high regularity.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: All spike trains contained a significantly higher number of regularly firing spikes than the control.
source: All of our spike trains contained a significantly higher number of regularly firing spikes (AI ≈ 0, or equivalently CV2 ≈ 0) than the control (p<0.01, one-sided z-test; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison with control data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ISI distributions had long tails that followed a power law with α = 3.78 ± 0.64.
source: ISI distributions had long tails that followed a power law, PISI(x) ~ x-α (α = 3.78 ± 0.64; tail onset = 30.4 ± 13.4 ms; p<0.05, n = 32) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical characterization of the ISI distribution from experimental data.

claim: The size of the ISI after each spike quickly diverged as the AI of the spike increased.
source: Furthermore, the size of the ISI after each spike quickly diverged as the AI of the spike increased (Figure 2C), implying that deviation from regular firing tends to be associated with long ISIs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and represents an observed relationship in the data.

claim: Deviation from regular firing tends to be associated with long ISIs.
source: Furthermore, the size of the ISI after each spike quickly diverged as the AI of the spike increased (Figure 2C), implying that deviation from regular firing tends to be associated with long ISIs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between AI and ISI size.

claim: Complex spikes had a larger average AI than simple spikes.
source: Complex spikes had a larger average AI than simple spikes (complex: 0.36 ± 0.12, simple: 5.9 × 10-4 ± 7.7 × 10-4), but their standard deviations were comparable (complex: 0.36 ± 0.05, simple: 0.31 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data.

claim: Correlations between AI and log10(ISI) were significantly smaller for complex spikes than simple spikes.
source: In all cells, correlations between AI and log10 (ISI) were significantly smaller for complex spikes than simple spikes (complex: 0.24 ± 0.15, simple: 0.66 ± 0.03; p<2.84 × 10-12, Wilcoxon rank-sum test), which made complex-spikes pauses poorly predicted by AI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the experimental data.

claim: Only 4.3 ± 2.5% of all pauses would be caused by complex spikes when selecting ~10% of all ISIs as representative pauses.
source: Therefore, if we select ~10% of all ISIs as representative 'pauses', based on ISI size and the AI value of a preceding spike (see below), only 4.3 ± 2.5% of all pauses would be caused by complex spikes.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data and selection criteria.

claim: The STALFP of spikes that initiated or terminated pauses was characterized by strong and sharp peaks around the spike time.
source: We found that the STALFP of spikes that initiated or terminated pauses was sharply different from those of regular spikes: the pause-related STALFP was characterized by strong and sharp peaks around the spike time, whereas the regular spike-related STALFP showed only a weak modulation (Figure 3A left, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and quantified in Figure 3B.

claim: Regular spike-related STALFP showed only a weak modulation.
source: We found that the STALFP of spikes that initiated or terminated pauses was sharply different from those of regular spikes: the pause-related STALFP was characterized by strong and sharp peaks around the spike time, whereas the regular spike-related STALFP showed only a weak modulation (Figure 3A left, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and quantified in Figure 3B.

claim: Pause spikes are more strongly and more precisely coupled to network activity than regular spikes.
source: This suggests that pause spikes are more strongly and more precisely coupled to network activity than regular spikes, but this fact goes unnoticed if the temporal structure of the spike train is ignored when computing the STALFP (Figure 3A right), because pauses are relatively rare events.
evidence: This is inferred from the STALFP analysis showing different coupling strengths.

claim: Pause spikes strongly preferred certain phases of the β/γ LFP while regular spikes showed only a weak dependence on the phase.
source: This was true in the entire dataset, where pause spikes strongly preferred certain phases of the β/γ LFP while regular spikes showed only a weak dependence on the phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the phase distribution analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Pause-initiating spikes preferentially occurred near the climbing phase at <φPauseI> = 48.7º ± 45.7º.
source: Notably, pause-initiating spikes preferentially occurred near the climbing phase, i.e., <φPauseI> = 48.7º ± 45.7º where φPauseI was the most preferred phase for each data set, and pause-terminating spikes were shifted by about 3/4 cycles on average (<φPauseT> = <φPauseI> + 278.3º ± 35.3º) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of phase preferences from the data.

claim: Pause-terminating spikes were shifted by about 3/4 cycles on average relative to pause-initiating spikes.
source: Notably, pause-initiating spikes preferentially occurred near the climbing phase, i.e., <φPauseI> = 48.7º ± 45.7º where φPauseI was the most preferred phase for each data set, and pause-terminating spikes were shifted by about 3/4 cycles on average (<φPauseT> = <φPauseI> + 278.3º ± 35.3º) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of phase relationships from the data.

claim: Pauses are not randomly occurring events.
source: These results clearly show that pauses are not randomly occurring events.
evidence: This is inferred from the phase-locking and STALFP results.

claim: Pause initiating and terminating spikes are temporally locked to specific patterns of network activity.
source: On the contrary, their initiating and terminating spikes are temporally locked to specific patterns of network activity, which generate significant and temporally precise fluctuations in the LFP.
evidence: This is inferred from the phase-locking and STALFP analyses.

claim: The β/γ LFP was significantly coherent across all saccades with phase locking to saccade onsets in many recordings.
source: In many of them, the β/γ LFP was significantly coherent across all saccades, with a phase locking to saccade onsets (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B and quantified by LFP phase reliability.

claim: Significantly high LFP phase reliability was found in 80% of the data.
source: Significantly high LFP phase reliability was found in 80% of the data (p<0.01, n = 28, one sided t-test to time-shifted control data; <RLFP> = 0.20 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Pause-initiating spikes encode saccade onsets with a significant and sharp increase in average firing.
source: The most significant pattern that we observed was that pause-initiating spikes encode saccade onsets with a significant and sharp increase in average firing (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spike reliability was significantly higher for pause spikes.
source: Significantly coincident spikes were indeed found during significant peaks of firing probability (colored regions in Figure 4C); therefore, spike reliability was significantly higher for pause spikes (Figure 4D), further emphasizing their role in encoding the onset of eye motion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D comparing spike reliability across spike types.

claim: The LFP phase and spike reliability were much more steeply related to each other for pause-initiating spikes than for regular spikes.
source: Finally, the LFP phase and spike reliability were much more steeply related to each other for pause-initiating spikes than for regular spikes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with different slopes for different spike types.

claim: The fidelity of temporal coding by pauses in individual PCs crucially reflects the reliability of activity and coding of the local network.
source: This demonstrates that the fidelity of temporal coding by pauses in individual PCs crucially reflects the reliability of activity and coding of the local network.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between LFP phase reliability and spike reliability.

claim: The linear rate prediction m followed the actual rate very closely with R2 = 0.92 ± 0.07.
source: We found that the linear rate prediction m followed the actual rate very closely (R2 = 0.92 ± 0.07, mean ± SD); therefore, the effect of the nonlinear transformation is small (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the linear-nonlinear model fitting.

claim: Correlation with the firing rate remained high (R2 = 0.81 ± 0.17) when computed with only regular spikes.
source: Importantly, correlation with the firing rate remained high (R2 = 0.81 ± 0.17) when we computed the linear prediction with only regular spikes, which comprised about 20% of all spikes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the linear model analysis with regular spikes only.

claim: The firing rate of pause spikes did not modulate as linearly or steeply as for regular spikes (R2 = 0.35 ± 0.25).
source: Conversely, the firing rate of pause spikes (both pause-initiating and –terminating spikes) did not modulate as linearly or steeply as for regular spikes (R2 = 0.35 ± 0.25).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the linear model analysis with pause spikes.

claim: When selecting ~47% of all spikes as regular spikes, their CCFSpike-EV is very similar (ρ ≈ 0.93 in average) to that of the full spike train.
source: For example, when we select ~47% of all spikes as regular spikes by imposing CV2 < 0.4, their CCFSpike-EV is very similar (ρ ≈ 0.93 in average) to that of the full spike train.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Regular spikes dominate rate coding.
source: The combination of Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrates that regular spikes dominate rate coding.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation between regular spike and full spike train rate coding.

claim: Regular spike and full spike trains respond to similar motion features and share the linear coding property.
source: Regular spike and full spike trains respond to similar motion features and also share the linear coding property.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in CCF patterns and R² values.

claim: Synchronized pauses can reliably trigger firing in CN neurons at movement onset.
source: Furthermore, recent optogenetic experiments have shown that synchronous pauses induced either by direct/indirect inhibition or at the offset of direct excitation, can reliably trigger firing in CN neurons, and importantly, at movement onset (Heiney et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to optogenetic studies.

claim: CN neurons can reliably generate time-locked rebound spikes in response to synchronized inputs followed by simultaneous disinhibition, even at moderate levels of synchrony (≤50%) and spike time jitter (≤20 ms).
source: With exceptionally fast GABAergic synapses (Person and Raman, 2012), CN neurons can reliably generate time-locked rebound spikes in response to synchronized inputs followed by simultaneous disinhibition, even at moderate levels of synchrony (≤50%) (Person and Raman, 2012) and spike time jitter (≤20 ms) (Gauck and Jaeger, 2000; Sudhakar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Synchronized pause spikes constitute the most significant population signal in PCs despite their sparse appearance in individual spike trains.
source: Our results show that synchronized pause spikes constitute the most significant population signal in PCs despite their sparse appearance in individual spike trains, suggesting that they can be a specific signaling mechanism in the PC-CN part of the motor pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong LFP coupling and reliability of pause spikes.

claim: Cerebellar LFP is coherent with neocortical LFP.
source: Considering that cerebellar LFP is coherent with neocortical LFP (Courtemanche and Lamarre, 2005; Soteropoulos and Baker, 2006; Ros et al., 2009) and also plays a critical role in maintaining LFP coherence between the sensory and motor cortex, particularly in the low γ band (Popa et al., 2013), pause spikes may also have a special relationship with the LFP in the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cerebellum plays a critical role in maintaining LFP coherence between the sensory and motor cortex, particularly in the low γ band.
source: Considering that cerebellar LFP is coherent with neocortical LFP (Courtemanche and Lamarre, 2005; Soteropoulos and Baker, 2006; Ros et al., 2009) and also plays a critical role in maintaining LFP coherence between the sensory and motor cortex, particularly in the low γ band (Popa et al., 2013), pause spikes may also have a special relationship with the LFP in the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Popa et al., 2013.

claim: The pause-related β/γ LFP signal originates from localized sources and decays quickly with distance, spreading at most a few hundred microns.
source: This suggests that the pause-related β/γ LFP signal originates from localized sources and decays quickly with distance, spreading at most a few hundred microns.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STALFP amplitude diminished in LFPs recorded ~1 mm away.

claim: PCs are rarely synchronized unless they are very close to each other (<100 μm).
source: This is consistent with the fact that PCs are rarely synchronized unless they are very close to each other (<100 μm) (Ebner and Bloedel, 1981; Jaeger, 2003; Shin and De Schutter, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The overall impact of complex spikes was negligible in this study.
source: The overall impact of complex spikes was negligible, most probably because none of our tasks involved sensorimotor learning where complex spikes are crucial (Catz et al., 2005; Medina and Lisberger, 2008), as they tend to occur after saccades, triggered by significant saccade errors (Herzfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the task design and supported by citations about complex spike function.

claim: In the motor and visual cortex, synchronized spikes have larger STALFP and better phase locking to the motion-related LFP β oscillation.
source: In the motor and visual cortex, synchronized spikes have larger STALFP and better phase locking to the motion-related LFP β oscillation (Denker et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in other brain regions.

claim: Firing rate variability and cross-correlation of PC firing both peaked at the onset of smooth-pursuit eye motion.
source: In another part of the cerebellum, Medina and Lisberger found that firing rate variability and cross-correlation of PC firing both peaked at the onset of smooth-pursuit eye motion (Medina and Lisberger, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Medina and Lisberger, 2007.

claim: Correlated spiking in PCs is due to common input to PCs.
source: Medina and Lisberger also suggested that such correlated spiking is due to common input to PCs (Medina and Lisberger, 2007), which can significantly contribute to the LFP signal (Denker et al., 2011) and trigger synchronized pauses (Jaeger, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Linear coding of motion kinematics by the PC firing rate has been repeatedly observed.
source: Linear coding of motion kinematics by the PC firing rate has been repeatedly observed (Shidara et al., 1993; Roitman et al., 2005; Medina and Lisberger, 2007; Herzfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: If correlations with other PCs are weak, rate coding by individual PCs can precisely control continuous movements since CN neurons receive inputs from many PCs and can average away noise in individual inputs.
source: If correlations with other PCs are weak, as is the case for regular spikes, rate coding by individual PCs can precisely control continuous movements since CN neurons receive inputs from many PCs and can average away noise in individual inputs.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about how rate coding works in the cerebellar circuit.

claim: Different stages of a movement may demand that some aspects of the motion be controlled more precisely than others.
source: Because different stages of a movement may demand that some aspects of the motion be controlled more precisely than others, it is useful for PCs to use different spike codes.
evidence: This is a general principle about motor control used to interpret the findings.

claim: Multiplexed coding is used for sensorimotor coordination in the cerebellar cortex.
source: We conclude that multiplexed coding is used for sensorimotor coordination in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.

claim: All animal experiments were approved by the local animal care committee (Protocol number: Regierungpräsidium Tübingen N1/08 and N6/13).
source: All animal experiments were approved by the local animal care committee (Protocol number: Regierungpräsidium Tübingen N1/08 and N6/13), conducted in accordance with German law and the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and carefully monitored by the veterinary administration (Regierungspräsidium and Landratsamt Tübingen).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the experiments.

claim: Three adult male rhesus monkeys were 10, 11, and 15 years old.
source: Three adult male rhesus (Macaca mulatta) monkeys (E, H, and N; 10, 11, and 15 years old, respectively) were subjects in this study.
evidence: This describes the age of the experimental subjects.

claim: Monkeys were implanted with a magnetic scleral search coil to record the eye position.
source: They were implanted with a magnetic scleral search coil to record the eye position (Judge et al., 1980), a titanium head post to painlessly immobilize the head during experiments, and a circular titanium recording chamber located over the midline of the cerebellum to allow electrophysiological recordings (Thier and Erickson, 1992).
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for the experiments.

claim: Animals made saccades either without (n = 16) or with visual cues (n = 18).
source: Animals made saccades either without (n = 16) or with visual cues (n = 18), but we analyzed all data combined.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigms used.

claim: Extracellular potentials were initially high- and low-pass filtered online and recorded separately.
source: Extracellular potentials were initially high- and low-pass filtered online and recorded separately.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: The band pass-filtered (300 Hz–3 kHz) channel was used to identify single-unit activity.
source: The band pass-filtered (300 Hz–3 kHz) channel was used to identify single-unit activity.
evidence: This describes the signal processing method for spike detection.

claim: Single-PC units were distinguished by the presence of simple and complex spikes via online sorting.
source: Single-PC units were distinguished by the presence of simple and complex spikes via online sorting, but all spikes were resorted offline and semi-automatically via a neural network trained on manually selected spike waveform prototypes as in (Yartsev et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting methodology.

claim: An additional offline low-pass filter at 42 Hz was applied to the LFP.
source: An additional offline low-pass filter at 42 Hz was applied.
evidence: This describes the LFP signal processing method.

claim: Eye velocity was computed from recorded eye position using a Savitzky-Golay filter of the fifth order with a 25 ms time window.
source: Eye velocity was computed from recorded eye position using a Savitzky-Golay filter of the fifth order with a 25 ms time window.
evidence: This describes the method for computing eye velocity.
